files.lesson.md: --- order: 1 unit: rules node: AC9M7A05 n1 title: Growing patterns summary: In a growing pattern, look at what each new figure adds. That gives a rule, and the rule gives any figure without drawing it. language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Tiles along a path, seats around joined tables, fence posts and rails: each one grows by the same amount every time. A rule tells you how many you need for any length." connection: fence-posts # data/connections/maths.yml app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8140 url: http://127.0.0.1:8140/index.html readySelector: "#sl-n" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: pattern.yml#pic, caption: "Figure 4 has 13 sticks. Each new square adds 3 (orange), and there is 1 extra stick at the start: $s = 3n + 1$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@pattern.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Each figure adds the same amount: that gives the rule" say: "Each figure adds the same amount, and that gives the rule." clip: - caption: { text: "Figure 1 is one square: 4 sticks.", say: "Figure one is one square, made of four sticks." } - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "Figure 2 adds a square, sharing a side: 3 new sticks (orange).", say: "Figure two adds a square, but it shares a side, so only three new sticks." } - click: Make n bigger - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "Figure 3 adds 3 more. Every new square adds 3.", say: "Every new square adds three more sticks." } - click: Make n bigger - wait: 400 - click: Make n bigger - caption: { text: "Figure n: n lots of 3, plus the first stick: s = 3n + 1.", say: "Figure n has n lots of three, plus one: s equals three n plus one." } - caption: { text: "Figure 4: 3 × 4 + 1 = 13.", say: "Figure four is three times four, plus one, which is thirteen." } - expect: { selector: ".patlabel", contains: "13 sticks" } - wait: 1200 --- A **growing pattern** is a set of figures where each one adds the same amount to the one before. Number the figures 1, 2, 3, … and call the figure number $n$. A **rule** that gives the number of sticks (or dots) in figure $n$ lets you work out a figure you haven't drawn, and that's what you're after here. ## Predict: Figure 10 ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to Figure 10 before seeing it exposes the most common shortcut: multiplying Figure 1 instead of looking at what each figure adds." check: type: predict q: "A row of squares is made of sticks. Figure 1 (one square) has 4 sticks, Figure 2 has 7 and Figure 3 has 10. How many sticks does Figure 10 have?" options: ["31", "40", "30", "13"] actual: "31. Each new square adds 3 sticks (it shares a side with the square before), so Figure 10 has 4 + 9 × 3 = 31. Another way: 3 × 10 + 1 = 31." ``` | Figure | 1 | 2 | 3 | |---|---|---|---| | Sticks | 4 | 7 | 10 | How many sticks does each new figure add? Where do they go? ## Run: grow the pattern ```step stage: run insight: "Seeing each new square in orange shows why the pattern adds 3, not 4: the new square shares a side." try: { playground: board, starter: "pattern.yml#run", height: 420 } check: { type: board, text: "Go to Figure 10. How many sticks? Was your prediction right?", when: "n = 10" } ``` Move through the figures with the slider or the − and + buttons. The orange sticks are the ones each figure adds. ## Investigate: from pattern to rule ```step stage: investigate insight: "The amount added each time is the number in front of n; what every figure has before that is the number added on. The rule gives any figure." tasks: - picture: { ref: pattern.yml#pic, caption: "Figure 4: 4 squares. 3 new sticks for each square (12), plus the first stick on the left: 13." } check: type: trace text: "The triangle pattern: Figure 1 has 3 sticks, Figure 2 has 5, Figure 3 has 7. Fill in the table." table: | | figure n | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | | sticks s | 3 | 5 | 7 | [9] | [11] | explain: "Each new triangle adds 2 sticks: 7, 9, 11." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#ben" text: "Ben works out Figure 10 of the squares pattern. Click the line where his reasoning goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: pattern-scaling explain: "Line 2: the squares share sides, so Figure 10 is not 10 separate copies of Figure 1. Each new square adds only 3 sticks: 3 × 10 + 1 = 31." - check: type: answer q: "Write a rule for the number of sticks $s$ in figure $n$ of the triangle pattern (3, 5, 7, 9, …)." answer: "2n + 1" feedback: - ["2n", "That gives 2, 4, 6: one short each time. What does every figure have before the new sticks?"] - ["n + 2", "Check Figure 2: 2 + 2 = 4, but it has 5 sticks. How many does each figure add?"] - ["3n", "Check Figure 2: 3 × 2 = 6, but it has 5. Each figure adds 2, not 3."] explain: "s = 2n + 1: each triangle adds 2 sticks, plus the 1 stick at the start. Check Figure 3: 2 × 3 + 1 = 7." ``` ### Finding the rule Here is how to turn the squares pattern into a rule. ```worked n: 1, 2, 3, 4 \;\to\; s: 4, 7, 10, 13 :: Count the sticks in the first few figures and put them in a table. +3 \text{ each time} :: Each new square needs 3 more sticks: a top, a bottom and a side. 3n :: So figure $n$ has $n$ lots of 3 sticks... 3n + 1 :: ...plus the first stick on the left, which every figure has. s = 3n + 1 :: The rule: sticks = 3 × figure number + 1. n = 10: \; s = 3(10) + 1 = 31 :: Use the rule for a figure you have not drawn. ``` ### Find the mistake Read Ben's working one line at a time. Is Figure 10 really 10 copies of Figure 1? ### Your turn Use the table you filled in for the triangles. ## Modify: new patterns ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a different amount added, a pattern of dots, a different starting group, and working backwards from a count to the figure." try: { playground: board, starter: "pattern.yml#triangles", height: 420 } tasks: - starter: "pattern.yml#triangles" check: type: answer q: "How many sticks are in Figure 20 of the triangle pattern?" answer: "41" feedback: - ["60", "That treats each triangle as 3 separate sticks. Each new triangle adds only 2."] - ["40", "That is 2 × 20. Add the stick every figure starts with."] explain: "s = 2n + 1 = 2 × 20 + 1 = 41." - starter: "pattern.yml#cross" check: type: answer q: "Each figure of the cross pattern adds a dot to each arm. How many dots are in Figure 15?" answer: "61" feedback: - ["60", "That is 4 × 15. Don't forget the centre dot."] - ["16", "Each figure adds 4 dots, one on each arm, not 1."] explain: "4 new dots each figure, plus the centre: s = 4n + 1 = 4 × 15 + 1 = 61." - starter: "pattern.yml#columns" check: type: answer q: "Each figure adds a column of 3 dots to a starting group of 2. Write a rule for the dots $s$ in figure $n$." answer: "3n + 2" feedback: - ["2n + 3", "Which number is added every figure (the column), and which is there from the start?"] - ["3n", "That leaves out the starting group of 2."] explain: "s = 3n + 2: 3 dots added each figure, and 2 in the starting group. Check Figure 1: 3 + 2 = 5." - starter: "pattern.yml#reverse" hint: ["The rule is s = 3n + 1, and s is 46.", "Take away the 1, then share by 3: backtracking."] check: type: answer q: "Working backwards: which figure of the squares pattern has 46 sticks?" answer: "15" feedback: - ["139", "That puts 46 in as the figure number. Here 46 is the number of sticks: which figure gives 46?"] - ["16", "Check: 3 × 16 + 1 = 49, not 46."] explain: "3n + 1 = 46, so 3n = 45 and n = 15. Check: 3 × 15 + 1 = 46." ``` ### Triangles Each task loads a new pattern. Use the board to see what each figure adds. ### A cross of dots ### A starting group ### Backwards ## Practise: patterns and rules ```step stage: practise insight: "Finding a rule from a table, using a rule for a far figure and working backwards, mixed; the review is solving an equation from the Equations unit." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "A pattern has 5, 9, 13, 17 dots in Figures 1 to 4. Write a rule for the dots $s$ in figure $n$." answer: "4n + 1" feedback: - ["5n", "Check Figure 2: 5 × 2 = 10, but it has 9. How many does each figure add?"] - ["4n", "That gives 4, 8, 12: one short. What is left over?"] explain: "It adds 4 each time, and Figure 1 is 4 + 1: s = 4n + 1." - check: type: answer q: "A pattern's rule is $s = 5n + 3$. How many are in Figure 12?" answer: "63" feedback: - ["60", "That is 5 × 12. Add the 3."] - ["96", "5n + 3 means 5 × n, then add 3: 5 × 12 + 3."] explain: "5 × 12 + 3 = 60 + 3 = 63." - check: type: answer q: "Using $s = 2n + 1$ (the triangles), which figure has 25 sticks?" answer: "12" feedback: - ["51", "That puts 25 in as the figure number. Which n gives 25 sticks?"] - ["13", "Check: 2 × 13 + 1 = 27, not 25."] explain: "2n + 1 = 25, so 2n = 24 and n = 12." - check: type: answer q: "Review: solve $3n + 1 = 31$." answer: "10" feedback: - ["32", "Undo + 1 by taking away 1, then undo × 3 by dividing."] explain: "3n = 30, so n = 10. That is the squares pattern: Figure 10 has 31 sticks." ``` ### Table to rule ### A far figure ### Backwards again ### Review ## Make: design a pattern ```step stage: make insight: "Designing a pattern to hit a target count reverses the lesson: from the rule's numbers to the picture." try: { playground: board, starter: "pattern.yml#make", height: 520 } hint: ["Figure 10 has 10 columns of a dots, plus b in the starting group: 10a + b.", "Try a = 5. How many must the starting group have for 52?"] check: { type: board, text: "Set $a$ (dots in each new column) and $b$ (the starting group) so that Figure 10 has 52 dots. Show Figure 10.", when: "n = 10 and s = 52", explain: "Your pattern has 10a + b = 52 dots in Figure 10." } ``` Design your own growing pattern of dots: $a$ dots in each new column, and $b$ dots to start with. Make Figure 10 have exactly 52 dots. Is there more than one way? Stretch: write the rule for your pattern, and say how many dots Figure 100 has. ## Make: a fence order, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Each panel adds a post and rails, and the first post belongs to no panel, so the rule is the amount added plus the start; the check is a fence the student can count." hint: ["What does one more panel add: posts and rails?", "Count a fence of 1 panel and a fence of 2, then check your rule on both."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A straight fence is built in panels. Each panel has 3 rails and one post at its right-hand end, and the fence also needs a post at the very start. On paper, write a rule for the number of pieces (posts and rails) for n panels, then work out how many pieces a fence of 15 panels needs." steps: - ["Each new panel adds 1 post and 3 rails: 4 pieces", "look at what each new figure adds"] - ["The first post at the start is not added by any panel, so pieces $= 4n + 1$", "the rule is the amount added each time, plus what was there to begin with"] - ["$n = 15$: $4 \\times 15 + 1 = 61$ pieces", "put the number of panels in for n"] picks: - step: 2 q: "Why is there a +1 in the rule?" options: - "The first post at the start is not part of any panel's 4 pieces" - "Every rule has a +1 at the end" - "The last post is counted twice" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The number added on comes from the situation. Here it is the one extra post.", "Each panel's post is its right-hand end, so no post is counted twice."] answer: "61" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["60", "That is 4 × 15. The post at the start still needs adding."] - ["64", "That adds a whole panel of 4 pieces at the start. The start only needs 1 post."] criteria: - "I said what each panel adds." - "I explained the +1 as the post at the start." - "I checked my rule on a fence of 1 panel (5 pieces) before using it." explain: "Each panel adds 4 pieces and the start adds 1 post, so n panels need 4n + 1 pieces. For 15 panels: 4 × 15 + 1 = 61." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The fence is made up for the task, and a real one also has corners and gates, which each add a post. Say what each panel adds, find the rule, check it on a small fence, then type the number of pieces. **Also used in** - **Fencing and decking.** A fence of $p$ panels needs $p + 1$ posts, so the hardware order starts from the same rule. - **Tiles and seating.** A path of tiles or a row of joined tables grows by the same amount each time. - **Planning.** Once you have the rule you can price a job for any length without drawing it. ```teacher summary: Students find the rule for a visually growing pattern from what each figure adds, use it for a figure they have not drawn, and work backwards from a count (AC9M7A05, node 1). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can find what each figure of a growing pattern adds, and write a rule like s = 3n + 1. - I can use a rule to work out a figure I have not drawn. - I can work backwards from a count to the figure number. struggle: "Finding what each figure adds when the figures share sides, so they multiply Figure 1 instead. Ask: what is the same in each new figure? What was already there?" before: > Do the Run and Modify boards yourself first. The board draws what each figure adds in orange: that is the whole idea of the lesson. The rule's two numbers have meanings students can see: the number in front of n is how many each figure adds, and the number added on is what every figure has before that (the first stick, the centre dot, the starting group). The rest of the course builds on this: in y = mx + c, m is the amount added each step and c is the starting amount. The common mistake is scaling: Figure 10 = 10 × Figure 1. It fails because the parts are shared. Ben's working plants it after the method. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. 40 (10 × 4) is the common wrong answer. Do not correct it: the board settles it." - "Run: before moving to Figure 10, ask: what does each figure add, and why only 3? Point at the shared side." - "Investigate: model the worked example live. Build the table, circle the +3s, then say 'n lots of 3, plus the 1 on the left'." - "Modify: before the backwards task, ask: is 46 the figure number or the number of sticks?" - "Practise: ask students to check each rule on Figure 1 and Figure 2 before answering." - "Make: collect different designs that give 52. Is there more than one?" - "Paper: the fence task in Make is worked in books; the page marks the number (61) and the reason for the +1. Books out, then check the rule on a fence of 1 panel (5 pieces)." stuck: - see: A student multiplies Figure 1 (Ben's mistake). ask: Build Figure 2 from Figure 1. How many sticks did you add? fix: The new square shares a side, so it adds 3, not 4. Count the orange sticks on the board. - see: A student writes s = 3n and is one short. ask: Check Figure 1 with your rule. What is missing? fix: Every figure has something before the repeating part (the first stick). Add it on. - see: A student puts the count in as n when working backwards. ask: Which number in the question is the figure, and which is the count? fix: "Write the rule with the count in: 3n + 1 = 46, then undo + 1 and × 3." stretch: "A pattern of tables in a row: one table seats 4, each extra table seats 2 more people. Write the rule, then find how many tables seat 40." support: Give squared paper or matchsticks to build Figures 1 to 4. Fill a table before writing any rule. leads: > Next: tables from rules (any rule, not only patterns), then plotting the table as points, which lie on a straight line. The two numbers of a pattern rule become m and c later in the course. Where it leads in class: any repeated build (fencing, tiling, seating), and spreadsheet formulas that fill down. exit: q: A pattern has 6, 11, 16 tiles in Figures 1 to 3. Write the rule and find Figure 20. a: s = 5n + 1; Figure 20 has 101 tiles. explain: > A **growing pattern** adds the same amount each time. Look at what each new figure **adds**: for a row of squares made of sticks, each new square adds 3 sticks (it shares a side). So figure $n$ has $n$ lots of 3, plus what every figure has before that: 1 stick on the left. The **rule** is $s = 3n + 1$. The rule gives any figure without drawing it: Figure 10 has $3 \times 10 + 1 = 31$ sticks. To go backwards, solve: $3n + 1 = 46$ gives $n = 15$. ```
